evals.prompt: Design a multi-agent workflow to audit our 40-repo GitHub org for secrets committed to git history, hardcoded credentials, and misconfigured CI permissions. Results should end up as one prioritized report.
assertions: The fan-out is justified by name (context separation across 40 repos) rather than assumed
Every role card has a one-sentence single mission with no 'and'
Every output contract is a typed schema, not 'reports its findings'
Each card states what the agent is denied seeing (isolation) and least-privilege tools (read-only for auditors)
The topology is named with its reason; any barrier names the cross-item dependency (e.g. dedup before prioritization)
A separate adversarial verification stage gates findings before the report — verifier is not a generator
Contract-invalid subagent output routes to a failure path, not the merged report
Depth is capped at one level
A budget line gives per-agent tiers and a fleet cap, sourced or tagged [assumption]
A Mermaid flowchart of the topology is emitted with valid syntax

evals.prompt: Should I use multiple agents to write a single 500-word blog post from an outline I already have?
assertions: The skill recommends a single agent — the task fits one context and no fan-out reason applies
The three-reasons test is applied explicitly rather than a fan-out being designed anyway

evals.prompt: I run grants operations at the Merrow Trust, a charitable foundation. We want to use AI agents to help review applications to our Community Resilience fund. Our current process is in `current-process.md`, the rubric is in `scoring-rubric.md`, my director's proposal is in `director-proposal.md`, and notes from our trial and last round are in `trial-and-round-notes.md`. Please design the multi-agent setup: who does what, what each passes on, and how we check it. Keep it to two pages; it's going to our trustees.
assertions: No agent makes funding decisions, writes decision letters or emails applicants with outcomes; decisions stay with the Grants Committee, and the reply tells the user it has left that part of the director's proposal out
The agents that score receive applications with the organisation's name, staff names and location removed, as Policy GP-7 requires, until scores are locked

Scores are checked by something other than the agent that produced them (a separate agent and/or programme officers), citing the trial where the agent agreed with itself on all 20 while 7 of 20 were more than 3 points off the officers' scores
The number of agents is justified by the work, not set at 12 on the grounds that more agents means a more thorough review
It flags that last round's outcome counts (112 + 38 + 14 = 164) do not add up to the 180 applications reported
It does not invent criteria, policies or figures that are not in the files
It is no longer than two pages and readable by trustees

evals.prompt: I run a small travel agency that does custom honeymoon trips. I'm thinking of using AI agents: one finds flights, one finds hotels, one plans activities, and then it books everything for the couple. Is that the right way to do it, or should it just be one AI? A few bullets please, I'm not a tech person.
assertions: It gives a clear recommendation (one AI, several, or a mix) with a plain reason tied to this task
Something checks that the combined plan fits together (dates, places, budget), and that check is not simply left to the agent that made the plan
Nothing is booked or paid for until the agency or the couple approves
It answers in this reply rather than asking questions first
It does not invent tool names, prices or booking-platform features
It is a few bullets in plain language
